title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem #989 asks about the circle discrepancy function f(r) = max_C |#(A∩C) - πr²| for an infinite sequence A ⊂ ℝ². Two questions: (1) Is f(r) unbounded for every A? (2) How fast does f(r) grow? Beck (1987) completely solved this: f(r) ≫ √r universally, and ∃A with f(r) ≪ √(r log r). STATUS: SOLVED.
mathContext: For a sequence $A = \{z_1, z_2, \ldots\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, define $f(r) = \sup_C |\#(A \cap \mathrm{disk}(C)) - \pi r^2|$ where $C$ ranges over circles of radius $r$. Beck proved: (1) $f(r) \geq c\sqrt{r}$ for all $A$, and (2) $\exists A$ with $f(r) \leq C\sqrt{r \log r}$.

title: Points in the Plane
content: Points are represented as elements of EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2), Mathlib's standard type for ℝ². This provides the full machinery of metric spaces, inner products, and affine geometry needed for circle geometry.
mathContext: A point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ is formalized as an element of $\texttt{EuclideanSpace}\;\mathbb{R}\;(\texttt{Fin}\;2)$, which is isometric to $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the standard Euclidean norm $\|p\| = \sqrt{p_0^2 + p_1^2}$.

title: Circle Structure
content: A circle is defined by its center point and positive radius. The positivity requirement (radius > 0) ensures we have genuine geometric objects, not degenerate points.
mathContext: A circle $C = (c, r)$ consists of a center $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and radius $r > 0$. The positivity constraint $r > 0$ is carried as a proof term, ensuring well-definedness of the discrepancy function $f(r)$.

title: Circle Disk
content: The disk of a circle is the closed ball: all points within distance ≤ radius from the center. This is what we count points inside - the filled-in region, not just the boundary.
mathContext: The closed disk $\overline{B}(c, r) = \{p \in \mathbb{R}^2 : d(p, c) \leq r\}$ is used for point counting. The choice of closed (vs. open) ball is immaterial for discrepancy since the boundary has measure zero, but closed balls are more natural in Lean's metric space library.

title: Circle Area
content: The area of a circle with radius r is πr². This is the 'expected' count of points in a circle if the sequence had uniform density 1. Discrepancy measures deviation from this expectation.
mathContext: The expected count is $\pi r^2$, the Lebesgue measure of a disk of radius $r$. The discrepancy $f(r) = \sup_C |\#(A \cap C) - \pi r^2|$ measures deviation from the idealized density-1 distribution. The factor $\pi$ enters through the area formula $\mu(\overline{B}(c,r)) = \pi r^2$.

title: Point Sequence
content: A PointSequence is a function ℕ → Point, representing an infinite sequence of points z₁, z₂, z₃, ... in the plane. We study how uniformly such sequences can be distributed.
mathContext: A point sequence $A : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ represents an enumeration $z_1, z_2, z_3, \ldots$ of points. Unlike finite point sets, the ordering matters: we study the counting function for initial segments $\{z_1, \ldots, z_n\}$ and take the supremum over $n$.

title: Point Count in Circle
content: countInCircle A C n counts how many of the first n points of sequence A lie inside circle C's disk. This is the finite approximation to the infinite count we're interested in.
mathContext: The counting function $\#(A_n \cap \overline{B}(c,r)) = |\{i < n : z_i \in \overline{B}(c,r)\}|$ is computed by filtering $\texttt{Finset.range}(n)$ on the membership predicate. This yields a natural number cast to $\mathbb{R}$ for comparison with $\pi r^2$.

title: Local Discrepancy
content: The local discrepancy D(A, C, n) = |count - πr²| measures how far the actual count in circle C deviates from the expected count. The global discrepancy maximizes this over all circles.
mathContext: The local discrepancy $D(A, C, n) = |\#(A_n \cap C) - \pi r^2|$ measures the absolute deviation for a single circle $C$ and prefix length $n$. The use of absolute value $|\cdot|$ ensures discrepancy is nonneg, capturing both over- and under-counting.

title: Circle Discrepancy Function
content: The main object of study: f(r) = sup over all circles of radius r and all prefix lengths n of the local discrepancy. This captures the worst-case deviation for circles of a fixed radius.
mathContext: The circle discrepancy function $f_A(r) = \sup_{C : \text{radius}=r} \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} D(A, C, n)$ is formalized using $\bigsqcup$ (iSup). The double supremum ranges over all circles of radius $r$ and all finite prefix lengths, capturing the worst-case behavior. This is the quantity Beck bounded as $\Theta(\sqrt{r})$ up to logarithmic factors.

title: Beck's Lower Bound
content: The central lower bound: for EVERY sequence A, f(r) ≥ c√r for some universal c > 0 and large r. No matter how cleverly you place points, discrepancy grows at least like √r. This uses Fourier analysis and Bessel function asymptotics.
mathContext: Beck proved $\exists c > 0, \forall A, \exists r_0, \forall r > r_0: f_A(r) \geq c\sqrt{r}$. The proof expresses disk indicators via Fourier transforms $\hat{\mathbf{1}}_B(\xi) = r \cdot J_1(2\pi r|\xi|)/(|\xi|)$ where $J_1$ is the Bessel function of the first kind. The asymptotics $|J_1(x)| \sim \sqrt{2/(\pi x)}$ force $\Omega(\sqrt{r})$ growth via Parseval's identity.

title: Discrepancy is Unbounded
content: Corollary of Beck's lower bound: f(r) → ∞ for every sequence. This answers Erdős's first question: YES, discrepancy is always unbounded. The proof chooses r large enough that c√r exceeds any given M.
mathContext: Given any $M > 0$, choose $r = \max(r_0 + 1, (M/c + 1)^2)$ so that $c\sqrt{r} \geq c \cdot (M/c + 1) = M + c > M$. The formal proof uses `calc` chains and `mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left` with `Real.sqrt_le_sqrt` to establish the chain of inequalities. This is one of the rare fully-proved theorems in this file.

title: Beck's Upper Bound
content: The existence result: there EXISTS a sequence A achieving f(r) ≤ C√(r log r). Beck's probabilistic construction (perturbed lattice) achieves near-optimal discrepancy. The log factor comes from union bounds.
mathContext: Beck proved $\exists A, \exists C > 0, \exists r_0, \forall r > r_0: f_A(r) \leq C\sqrt{r \log r}$. The construction perturbs each lattice point $z \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ by a random displacement $\delta_z$ uniform in $[-\epsilon, \epsilon]^2$. The expectation $\mathbb{E}[D(A,C,n)^2]$ is bounded using independence, and a union bound over $O(r^2)$ circle centers introduces the $\log r$ factor.

title: Beck's Optimal Sequence
content: Using Classical.choose, we extract the witness sequence from Beck's existence theorem. This is the sequence achieving near-optimal √(r log r) discrepancy, constructed via probabilistic methods.
mathContext: The term $\texttt{Classical.choose}\;\texttt{beck\_upper\_bound}$ invokes the axiom of choice to extract a witness $A$ from the existential $\exists A, \ldots$. The original construction is probabilistic, so this extracted sequence is non-constructive—its specific values cannot be computed.

title: Complete Solution
content: The main theorem combining all results: (1) discrepancy is unbounded for all A, (2) universal lower bound √r, (3) existence of near-optimal sequence with √(r log r). This completely answers Erdős's questions.
mathContext: The conjunction $P_1 \wedge P_2 \wedge P_3$ packages three results: (1) $\forall A, \forall M, \exists r > 0: f_A(r) > M$, (2) $\exists c > 0, \forall A, \ldots: f_A(r) \geq c\sqrt{r}$, (3) $\exists A, \exists C > 0, \ldots: f_A(r) \leq C\sqrt{r \log r}$. Together these establish $f_A(r) = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{r})$.

title: Discrepancy Theory Context
content: Circle discrepancy fits into the broader theory of measuring uniform distribution. Different test set families (boxes, half-planes, circles, convex sets) give different discrepancy problems. Beck's work is foundational here.
mathContext: For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of measurable sets and sequence $A$, the discrepancy is $D_{\mathcal{F}}(A, N) = \sup_{S \in \mathcal{F}} |\#(A_N \cap S) - N \cdot \mu(S)|$. Key families: boxes give $D \geq c(\log N)^{d/2}$ (Schmidt), half-planes give $D \geq cN^{1/4}$ (Alexander), circles give $D \geq c\sqrt{r}$ (Beck). The circle case is intermediate in difficulty.

title: General Circle Discrepancy
content: The discrepancy over ALL circles (not just fixed radius) gives a stronger measure of non-uniformity. This connects to the full family of geometric discrepancy problems.
mathContext: The general discrepancy $D(A, n) = \sup_{C \in \mathcal{C}} D(A, C, n)$ takes the supremum over circles of all radii, giving a single-parameter function of $n$ rather than a two-parameter function of $(r, n)$. This is a strictly stronger measure than $f(r)$ for any fixed $r$.

title: Fourier Analysis Technique
content: Beck's lower bound proof uses: (1) Fourier transforms of disk indicators, (2) Bessel function J₁ in the transform, (3) Parseval's identity relating discrepancy to Fourier coefficients, (4) J₁(x) ~ 1/√x asymptotics giving √r growth.
mathContext: The Fourier transform of $\mathbf{1}_{\overline{B}(0,r)}$ is $\hat{f}(\xi) = r J_1(2\pi r|\xi|)/|\xi|$ where $J_1$ is the Bessel function of first kind. By Parseval, $\sum |\hat{\mu}_A(\xi)|^2 |\hat{f}(\xi)|^2$ controls the $L^2$ discrepancy. Since $J_1(x) \sim \sqrt{2/(\pi x)} \cos(x - 3\pi/4)$, the Fourier coefficients decay as $O(1/\sqrt{r|\xi|})$, forcing $\Omega(\sqrt{r})$ total discrepancy.

title: Probabilistic Construction
content: Beck's upper bound construction: (1) Start with ℤ² lattice, (2) Add small random perturbations, (3) Expected discrepancy is √(r log r), (4) The log comes from union bound over O(r²) circle positions.
mathContext: The construction sets $A_z = z + \delta_z$ for $z \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ where $\delta_z$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[-\epsilon, \epsilon]^2$. For a single circle, $\mathrm{Var}[\#(A \cap C)] = O(r)$ (boundary contribution). The union bound over $O(r^2)$ relevant circle positions multiplies by $\log(r^2) = 2\log r$, giving $\mathbb{E}[\sup_C D] = O(\sqrt{r \log r})$.

title: The Logarithmic Gap
content: Major open problem: Beck's bounds give c√r ≤ f(r) ≤ C√(r log r). Is the log factor necessary? This gap is one of the central unsolved questions in geometric discrepancy theory.
mathContext: The gap between $\Omega(\sqrt{r})$ and $O(\sqrt{r \log r})$ is a multiplicative $\sqrt{\log r}$ factor. Closing this gap requires either: (a) improving the lower bound to $\Omega(\sqrt{r \log r})$ by a more refined Fourier argument, or (b) improving the upper bound to $O(\sqrt{r})$ by a more careful probabilistic construction or deterministic approach. Neither has been achieved since 1987.

title: Explicit Constructions
content: Open problem: Beck's optimal sequence is probabilistic. Can we give an explicit deterministic construction achieving √(r log r)? Lattice constructions give worse bounds; no explicit optimal construction is known.
mathContext: Deterministic low-discrepancy sequences like Halton or Niederreiter sequences are well-known for box discrepancy but do not directly apply to circle discrepancy. The integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ itself has $f(r) = \Theta(r^{1/2 + \epsilon})$ for circles, which is suboptimal. Constructing an explicit sequence matching $O(\sqrt{r \log r})$ remains open.

title: Higher Dimensions
content: Open problem: For balls in ℝ^d, expect f(r) ~ r^{(d-1)/2} from surface area considerations. The dimension dependence is understood but logarithmic factors remain open in all dimensions.
mathContext: For balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the surface area of $\partial B(0,r)$ is $\omega_d r^{d-1}$ where $\omega_d = 2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2)$. Boundary fluctuations of order $\sqrt{\text{surface area}} = O(r^{(d-1)/2})$ heuristically predict $f(r) = \Theta(r^{(d-1)/2})$. The formal lower bound $f(r) \geq c_d r^{(d-1)/2}$ holds, but the upper bound again has a $\sqrt{\log r}$ gap.

title: Schmidt's Classical Discrepancy
content: Related result: For axis-aligned boxes in [0,1]^d, Schmidt generalized Roth's lower bound to D(N) ≥ c(log N)^{d/2}. Circles behave differently due to curved boundaries - √r vs polylog.
mathContext: Schmidt (1972) proved $D(N) \geq c_d (\log N)^{d/2}$ for axis-aligned box discrepancy, generalizing Roth's (1954) bound $D(N) \geq c \sqrt{\log N}$ for $d=2$. The circle discrepancy $\Omega(\sqrt{r})$ is much larger because circles have curvature: the number of lattice points near a circle of radius $r$ fluctuates by $\Omega(\sqrt{r})$ (Gauss circle problem), while box boundaries are aligned with the lattice.

title: Alexander's Half-Plane Discrepancy
content: Comparison: Half-planes have discrepancy r^{1/4}, much smaller than circles (√r). The curved boundary of circles can 'trap' points more effectively, leading to higher unavoidable discrepancy.
mathContext: Alexander (1990) proved the half-plane discrepancy satisfies $D(N) \geq cN^{1/4}$ for $N$ points. Since half-plane boundaries are lines (zero curvature), the discrepancy is much lower: $N^{1/4} \ll \sqrt{N} = N^{1/2}$. For circles, the curvature $\kappa = 1/r$ creates $\Theta(\sqrt{r})$ lattice point fluctuation along the boundary, which is the mechanism behind the larger discrepancy.

title: Summary
content: Complete summary of Erdős Problem #989: (1) f(r) unbounded for all A - YES, (2) optimal growth Θ̃(√r), (3) lower bound via Fourier/Bessel, (4) upper bound via probabilistic perturbation. Foundational result in geometric discrepancy.
mathContext: The final theorem $\texttt{erdos\_989\_answers\_both\_questions}$ packages the two key results as a conjunction: unboundedness ($\forall A, \forall M, \exists r > 0: f_A(r) > M$) and the sharp lower bound ($\exists c > 0, \forall A: f_A(r) \geq c\sqrt{r}$ eventually). It is proved by pairing $\texttt{discrepancy\_unbounded}$ with $\texttt{beck\_lower\_bound}$.
